claim: Portugal's failure to reconquer Ceylon after the VOC completed the seizure of its remaining island fortifications in 1658 is best explained as a constrained imperial reallocation after military defeat: the Estado da Índia faced a damaged Cape-route logistics system, simultaneous pressure across Asia and the post-1640 Braganza Restoration crisis, while the VOC consolidated the captured ports and peace with Portugal was ratified in 1663. This was not an immediate voluntary abandonment: Van Goens still feared a Portuguese counter-offensive in 1661.
bounded_by: Do not reduce non-return to one Atlantic-profit decision. Atlantic/Brazilian pressures belong to the wider allocation environment, but the directly anchored mechanism here is military loss plus degraded Asian logistics, multi-front constraints, Braganza-state reorganization, Dutch fortification/consolidation and the 1661–1663 peace sequence. Ames also shows that the Estado stabilized later, so this is contraction and reprioritization, not total Portuguese Asian collapse.
notes: Narrative bridge: 1658 Ceylon loss → 1661 still-feared counteroffensive → 1663 peace/reconfiguration → surviving reduced Estado elsewhere in Asia. Refines C-PRE-GEO-002.
